deep.reconstruction:
Context: this page belongs to a run of tables (previous page: p = 101, 109, 113, 137, 149; next page: 293, 281). They are Gauss's tables of biquadratic (quartic) residue classes, the material behind Theoria residuorum biquadraticorum (1828/1832).

The scheme for each prime p ≡ 1 (mod 4):
- g is a primitive root.
- f = g^((p-1)/4) mod p, so f^2 ≡ -1.
- (a,b) is written 'a + b i' with p = a^2 + b^2, b even, a ≡ 1 (mod 4), and the sign chosen so that a + b f ≡ 0 (mod p). With π = a + bi this means i ≡ f (mod π).
- Each x with 1 ≤ x ≤ p-1 is placed by its index mod 4. Class A means ind x ≡ 0, i.e. x^((p-1)/4) ≡ 1 (the biquadratic residues). Classes B, C, D mean ind x ≡ 1, 2, 3, i.e. x^((p-1)/4) ≡ f, -1, -f.
- Equivalently, the class of x is the quartic symbol [x/π] = 1, i, -1, -i.

(1) p = 157, g = 5, f = 129, 'a+bi' = -11-6i.
- 129^2 = 16641 = 106·157 - 1. Also 5^4 ≡ -3, 5^8 ≡ 9, 5^16 ≡ 81, 5^32 ≡ 124, so 5^39 ≡ 129.
- 157 = 11^2 + 6^2, and -11 - 6·129 = -785 = -5·157.
- All four classes are written out in full (39 each). Since p ≡ 5 (mod 8), -1 ∈ C, so C = -A and D = -B. Gauss's lists satisfy this except for one slip (see errors).

(2) p = 173, g = 2, f = 80, 13+2i.
- 2^43 ≡ 80 and 13 + 2·80 = 173.
- Only 1 ≤ x ≤ 86 are listed, since -x lies two classes further on. In that range |A| + |C| = 43 and |B| + |D| = 43.
- I checked every composite entry by index additivity; all are consistent.

(3) p = 181, g = 2, f = 162, 9+10i.
- 2^45 ≡ 162 and 9 + 10·162 = 9·181.
- Listed for x ≤ 90: |A| = 29, |B| = 27, |C| = 16, |D| = 18 (A+C = B+D = 45). Every composite entry checks.
- In C some entries are struck through and re-entered in D; for example 17 ∈ D, because 34 = 2·17 ∈ A and 2 ∈ B.

(4) p = 193, g = 5, f = 112, -7-12i.
- 112^2 ≡ -1 and -7 - 12·112 = -7·193.
- p ≡ 1 (mod 8), so -1 ∈ A and each class has 24 members ≤ 96.
- D needs both the interlined 44 and the overwritten 51 (51 = 3·17 with 3 ∈ A, 17 ∈ D), plus the bracketed 87 = 3·29. With these, all 96 numbers are accounted for.
- 2 ∈ C here, in agreement with Gauss's rule for 2 (b = 12 ≡ 4 mod 8).

(5) Bottom table: the classes of +3 and -3 for every prime p ≡ 1 (mod 4) from 5 to 173. The source rows for 101–149 are on the previous page; I checked those against it and they agree.
- +3: A = {13, 109}; B = {17, 29, 53, 89, 101, 113, 137}; C = {37, 61, 73, 97, 157}; D = {5, 41, 149, 173}.
- -3: A = {37, 61, 157}; B = {5, 17, 89, 113, 137, 149, 173}; C = {13, 73, 97, 109}; D = {29, 41, 53, 101}.
- Consistency: -1 is in A for p ≡ 1 (mod 8) and in C for p ≡ 5 (mod 8), so class(-3) = class(3) or class(3) + 2. All 18 entries satisfy this.
- The data instantiate the law [-3/π] ≡ π^2 (mod 3) (my identification). This follows from biquadratic reciprocity, since -3 is primary and N(-3) = 9, so the sign factor is 1.
- Checks: 157: π^2 = 85+132i ≡ 1, so -3 ∈ A. 173: 165+52i ≡ i, so B. 101: -99+20i ≡ -i, so D. 109: -91-60i ≡ -1, so C. 113 and 137: ≡ i, so B. 149: ≡ i, so B.
- Hence -3 ∈ A iff 3 | b, and -3 ∈ C iff 3 | a (for p ≡ 1 mod 12). For p ≡ 5 (mod 12), B or D is fixed by ab mod 3.
- The page's own rows for 181 (3 ∈ A) and 193 (3 ∈ A) also obey this, but they were not entered in the bottom table. The table was probably compiled before those rows.

Purpose: collecting numerical evidence for the biquadratic character of ±3 in terms of the decomposition p = a^2 + b^2, parallel to Gauss's published treatment of 2.
errors: p = 157, class A contains 107 and omits 75; class C contains 50 and omits 82. In fact 75 = 3·5^2 has index ≡ 2+1+1 ≡ 0, so 75 ∈ A and 82 = -75 ∈ C. Also 50 = 2·5^2 ∈ D (index 1+2 = 3), and 107 = -50 ∈ B. Gauss's entries 107 in B and 50 in D are therefore correct, and the A/C entries 107/50 are slips for 75/82. Without the correction, 107 and 50 appear twice and the pair {75, 82} is missing.
p = 193, class D: the interlined 44 and the overwritten 51 must both stand (D then has 24 members). The bracketed 87 is also correct.
p = 181, class C: the struck-out entries are correct deletions. 17 belongs in D.
The bottom ±3 table omits p = 181 and 193, although the page's own rows give 3 ∈ A for both. This is incompleteness, not an error.

results.what: Tables of the four biquadratic residue classes A, B, C, D modulo p = 157, 173, 181, 193, defined by a primitive root g and f = g^((p-1)/4), with p = a^2 + b^2 normalized by a ≡ 1 (mod 4) and a + b f ≡ 0 (mod p)
results.modern_name: quartic residue classes / quartic residue symbol [x/π] for π | p in Z[i]

results.what: Biquadratic class of +3 and -3 for all primes p ≡ 1 (mod 4) up to 173; the data obey [-3/π] = π^2 mod 3 (-3 ∈ A iff 3 | b, C iff 3 | a; B/D according to ab mod 3)
results.modern_name: quartic character of 3 (a special case of quartic reciprocity)
results.usually_credited_to: Quartic reciprocity was stated by Gauss (1832) and proved by Jacobi (lectures 1836/37) and Eisenstein (1844); explicit criteria for small primes appear in Gauss's Nachlass, Dirichlet, and later Lehmer (1958)

deep.surprise_reason: These are computational tables of exactly the kind underlying Gauss's published work on biquadratic residues, with the A/B/C/D classes and the a + bi normalization known from his memoirs and Nachlass. The ±3 summary is empirical groundwork for a law that follows from the reciprocity law he announced. Nothing here goes beyond what is attributed to him.
